missions.name: Salvation Army and Holiness missions (Booth, Booth-Tucker in India, Keswick)
missions.statusNote: The Salvation Army works in more than 130 countries and is one of the world’s largest non-governmental providers of social services; its evangelistic and social wings remain intertwined. Holiness denominations (Nazarenes, Wesleyans, Free Methodists, the Christian and Missionary Alliance) continue as international churches whose membership is now mostly outside North America, while the Keswick Convention survives as an annual Bible-teaching gathering rather than a missionary engine.
missions.summary: A cluster of nineteenth-century movements, rooted in Methodist teaching on entire sanctification and in the ‘higher life’ spirituality of Keswick, that turned holiness piety into a missionary force. William and Catherine Booth’s Salvation Army carried a uniformed, quasi-military evangelism and social work from the East End of London to India, Africa, Asia and the Americas; Frederick Booth-Tucker adopted Indian dress and begging bowls in Bombay. Keswick sent a stream of volunteers into the CMS and faith missions, and American holiness churches built their own mission networks.
missions.story:
The holiness movement grew out of John Wesley’s teaching that believers could be made perfect in love in this life. In the United States Phoebe Palmer’s ‘altar theology’ (1830s–1870s) made entire sanctification an instantaneous, attainable experience, and camp meetings of the National Camp Meeting Association (from 1867) spread it across Methodism. In Britain the American lay preachers Robert Pearsall Smith and Hannah Whitall Smith led ‘higher life’ meetings at Broadlands and Oxford (1874) and Brighton (1875), and the vicar of Keswick, T. D. Harford-Battersby, began the Keswick Convention in 1875. Keswick taught a less Wesleyan, ‘counteraction’ view of victory over sin, but shared the conviction that a consecrated life should be poured out in service — and from the 1880s that increasingly meant overseas mission.

William Booth, a former Methodist New Connexion minister, began open-air preaching in Whitechapel in 1865 with his wife Catherine, a forceful advocate of women’s preaching. The East London Christian Mission was renamed The Salvation Army in 1878; it adopted ranks, uniforms, flags, brass bands and a ‘General’, and in 1883 stopped celebrating baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Its rowdy processions provoked the ‘Skeleton Army’ riots in English towns and bans in Switzerland, but it grew fast. George Scott Railton and seven women ‘lasses’ opened work in New York in 1880; officers reached Australia (1880), France and Canada (1881–82), India, Sweden and Switzerland (1882), South Africa, Ceylon and New Zealand (1883), and later Japan (1895), Korea (1908), Nigeria (1920), Kenya (1921), the Gold Coast (1922) and the Belgian Congo (1934). Booth’s In Darkest England and the Way Out (1890), drafted with W. T. Stead, set out a scheme of shelters, labour bureaux and farm colonies that defined the Army’s social mission.

India was its most distinctive experiment. Frederick Tucker, a former Indian Civil Service officer, landed at Bombay in September 1882 with three companions. The party wore Indian dress, went barefoot, took Indian names (Tucker became ‘Fakir Singh’), lived on alms and preached in the vernacular, a deliberate imitation of the sadhu that won attention among villagers in Gujarat, Punjab and the south but also arrests in Bombay for street processions. Tucker married Booth’s daughter Emma in 1888 and took the name Booth-Tucker. On his return to lead the Indian work (1907–1919) the Army took on a role that has since attracted sharp criticism: from 1908 it managed settlements for communities labelled ‘criminal tribes’ under the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871, running agricultural and industrial colonies in the United Provinces, Punjab and Madras on behalf of the colonial state.

Keswick’s missionary influence ran through other bodies. The ‘Cambridge Seven’ who joined the China Inland Mission in 1885 were steeped in its piety; the Keswick missionary meeting (from 1886) and the ‘Keswick missioner’ scheme sent people such as Amy Carmichael (to Japan in 1893 and India in 1895) and shaped the CMS ‘Keswick men’ on the Niger in the late 1880s. In America the holiness churches organised their own missions: the Christian and Missionary Alliance (A. B. Simpson, 1887), the Church of the Nazarene (united at Pilot Point, Texas, in 1908), the Free Methodists and Wesleyan Methodists, and the Oriental Missionary Society of Charles and Lettie Cowman and Ernest Kilbourne, which began in Tokyo in 1901 and grew into the Korea Evangelical Holiness Church after 1907.

The holiness emphasis on a second, crisis experience of the Spirit fed directly into Pentecostalism after 1901, and many holiness congregations, especially in the American South and in India, became Pentecostal; others reacted strongly against tongues. In the twentieth century the Salvation Army increasingly became known as a relief and welfare agency — hostels, disaster response, addiction services, hospitals such as Catherine Booth Hospital in Nagercoil (1893) — while still describing itself as an evangelical church. It has faced institutional-abuse findings in children’s homes, notably before Australia’s Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse (2014–15), and recurring controversy over its teaching on sexuality.

The holiness missions left large churches in the global South: by the early twenty-first century most Salvationists lived in Africa and Asia, with India, Kenya, Zimbabwe, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Papua New Guinea among its largest territories, and the Church of the Nazarene and the C&MA reported a majority of members outside the United States. Historians credit the movement with pioneering women’s public ministry and with fusing evangelism to practical social care, while noting its paternalism and its readiness to serve imperial governments.
beliefs: Entire sanctification or ‘full salvation’: a second work of grace, after conversion, cleansing the heart and enabling a life of perfect love (Wesleyan holiness, Salvation Army)
Keswick ‘higher life’ teaching: victory over known sin by continual surrender and faith, without the claim that the sinful nature is eradicated
Holiness expressed in service: consecration was expected to lead to evangelism, rescue work and overseas mission
Equality of women in ministry: Catherine Booth’s Female Ministry (1859) and Salvation Army practice gave women officers equal rank in preaching and command
Non-observance of baptism and the Lord’s Supper in the Salvation Army (from 1883), holding that inward grace does not depend on outward rites
Strong conversionist urgency combined with belief that social salvation (‘soup, soap and salvation’) was part of the gospel
strategies: Military organisation: territories, corps, ranks, uniforms, flags and brass bands to attract attention and build discipline
Open-air preaching, street processions and ‘invasions’ of new towns by small teams of officers
Identification with the poor: Booth-Tucker’s team in India adopted Indian dress, names, bare feet and begging
Social institutions: shelters, rescue homes for women, labour colonies, hospitals, leprosy work and disaster relief
Conventions and consecration meetings (Keswick, National Camp Meeting Association) that recruited missionaries
Self-funded denominational boards for holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan, Free Methodist, C&MA) sending missionaries alongside national evangelists
groupsReached: The urban poor, alcoholics and prostitutes of industrial Britain, the United States and Australia
Rural and low-caste communities in Gujarat, Punjab and Tamil Nadu, including Dalits and communities labelled ‘criminal tribes’
Japanese and Korean urban populations through the Oriental Missionary Society (Korea Evangelical Holiness Church)
Communities in southern and eastern Africa — Zimbabwe, Kenya, Zambia, Congo — where the Salvation Army became a large church
Indigenous and Caribbean peoples served by the C&MA, Nazarene and Wesleyan missions in Latin America
Lepers, orphans and displaced people through medical and relief institutions
challenges: Mob violence and legal bans: the ‘Skeleton Army’ riots in England (1880s), expulsions from Swiss cantons, arrests in Bombay (1882–83)
Disease and early deaths among officers living in Indian style on alms
Tension between evangelistic aims and the growing weight of social and relief institutions
Holiness divisions over tongues after 1906, which split congregations and missions
Dependence on colonial authorities for land, grants and permission to operate
Financial strain and authoritarian governance under a single General, leading to schisms (e.g. Ballington and Maud Booth’s Volunteers of America, 1896)
harms: In India the Salvation Army administered ‘criminal tribe’ settlements for the colonial government (from 1908), participating in a system of surveillance, restricted movement and compulsory labour imposed on whole communities
Paternalism: officers from Britain long monopolised senior command in mission territories, and indigenous leadership was slow to be promoted
Abuse of children in Salvation Army homes in Australia, Canada and Britain, documented by public inquiries in the 2000s–2010s
Holiness perfectionism produced cases of spiritual pressure, guilt and harsh discipline, and some rejection of medicine in faith-healing wings
Clashes with local religious communities and with other churches over aggressive street evangelism and ‘sheep-stealing’
developments: Pioneered large-scale equality of women in preaching and leadership decades before most denominations
Built a worldwide network of hostels, hospitals, schools, leprosy and disaster-relief services
Booth-Tucker’s adoption of Indian dress and lifestyle was an early Protestant experiment in identification with local culture
Keswick spirituality shaped generations of evangelical missionaries, including the Cambridge Seven and Amy Carmichael
Holiness churches in Korea, Japan, Africa and Latin America became self-governing national churches
The holiness ‘second blessing’ framework supplied the theological seedbed for Pentecostalism
missions.outcome: The holiness missions produced international churches whose centre of gravity has shifted to Africa, Asia and Latin America, and made the Salvation Army a global welfare institution. Their pairing of personal holiness with social action endured, as did criticism of their colonial entanglements and institutional failures.

missions.name: Azusa Street and the Pentecostal missionary explosion (Garr, Assemblies of God, global Pentecostalism)
missions.statusNote: Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity is the fastest-growing form of Christianity of the past century; the World Christian Database estimates well over 600 million adherents in the 2020s, though totals depend heavily on how ‘charismatic’ is defined. Most adherents live in Africa, Latin America and Asia and belong to nationally founded churches rather than missions.
missions.summary: Beginning with Charles Parham’s Bible school in Topeka (1901) and William J. Seymour’s Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles (1906–09), Pentecostals taught that Spirit baptism, evidenced by speaking in tongues, empowered believers for world evangelisation before Christ’s imminent return. Within a few years missionaries had gone from Azusa Street and its satellite revivals to India, China, Africa, Scandinavia and South America, and the Assemblies of God (1914) built one of the largest mission organisations of the century. The movement’s later explosive growth was driven above all by indigenous preachers.
missions.story:
Pentecostalism was missionary from the start. At Charles Fox Parham’s Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Kansas, Agnes Ozman spoke in tongues on 1 January 1901, and Parham taught that this gift was xenolalia — real foreign languages bestowed so that missionaries could preach abroad without study. In Houston in 1905 Parham’s segregated classes were attended, from the corridor, by William J. Seymour, an African American holiness preacher. Seymour carried the message to Los Angeles, and from April 1906 the Apostolic Faith Mission at 312 Azusa Street drew black, white, Latino and Asian worshippers in meetings that ran almost continuously until about 1909. Its paper, The Apostolic Faith, sent free to tens of thousands of readers, reported that ‘Pentecost has come’ and announced missionaries leaving for the ends of the earth.

The first wave of ‘missionaries of the one-way ticket’ left within months. Alfred G. Garr and Lillian Garr, believing they had received Bengali and Chinese, sailed for India and reached Calcutta at the end of 1906; finding that their tongues were not intelligible, they preached in English among missionaries and Anglo-Indians, helped spread Pentecostal experience in missionary circles, and went on to Hong Kong in 1907. Others went to Liberia, Angola and China. The disappointment of xenolalia led most Pentecostals to reinterpret tongues as prayer languages, but the conviction of empowerment for mission remained. Revivals elsewhere — the Welsh revival (1904–05), Pandita Ramabai’s Mukti Mission near Pune (1905), and the Korean revival (1907) — showed that the movement had multiple origins.

The experience spread by networks of holiness and evangelical periodicals. The Methodist Thomas Ball Barratt, having received Spirit baptism in New York, brought it to Kristiania (Oslo) in December 1906, and from there it reached Sweden (Lewi Pethrus’s Filadelfia church, Stockholm), Britain (Alexander Boddy in Sunderland, 1907) and Germany. Swedish Baptists Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, influenced in Chicago by William Durham, landed at Belém in November 1910; their split from the local Baptist church in 1911 began what became the Assembleias de Deus, now Brazil’s largest Protestant church. Willis Hoover’s Methodist congregation in Valparaíso experienced revival in 1909, producing the Methodist Pentecostal Church of Chile. In South Africa John G. Lake and Thomas Hezmalhalch founded the Apostolic Faith Mission in 1908, whose Zionist offshoots fed into African independent churches.

Organisation followed. The Church of God in Christ (C. H. Mason, 1907) and the Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee) became Pentecostal; the Assemblies of God was founded at Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914, with a strong emphasis on foreign missions, and adopted Roland Allen-style ‘indigenous church’ principles, systematised by Melvin Hodges in The Indigenous Church (1953). The Oneness controversy split the movement in 1916, and racial division hardened: the Assemblies of God was overwhelmingly white, and the Pentecostal Fellowship of North America (1948) excluded black churches until its dissolution and replacement in the ‘Memphis Miracle’ of 1994. British Pentecostals formed the Elim (1915) and Assemblies of God (1924) churches, with missions in Africa and India.

After 1945 the decisive growth came from national leaders and churches: the Church of Pentecost in Ghana (from James McKeown’s work, 1937), the Redeemed Christian Church of God (Nigeria, 1952), David Yonggi Cho’s Yoido Full Gospel Church in Seoul (1958), the Indian Pentecostal Church of God (1924) and Ceylon Pentecostal Mission, and Chinese house churches with strongly charismatic practice. Healing evangelists such as T. L. Osborn and Reinhard Bonnke drew vast crowds in Africa, while the charismatic renewal from 1960 carried Pentecostal experience into the historic Protestant and Catholic churches. Neo-Pentecostal megachurches, often teaching prosperity, multiplied in Latin America and Africa from the 1980s.

Scholars such as Allan Anderson and Walter Hollenweger argue that Pentecostalism’s growth owes most to its oral, participatory worship, its translation of the gospel into local idioms of spiritual power, healing and deliverance, and its openness to lay and women preachers. Critics point to the prosperity gospel, authoritarian ‘big man’ leadership, financial scandals, witchcraft accusations in deliverance ministries, and political alliances with strongmen. The movement now sends missionaries from Brazil, Nigeria, Korea and elsewhere throughout the world.
beliefs: Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, classically evidenced by speaking in tongues (the ‘initial evidence’ doctrine)
The ‘full gospel’: Jesus as saviour, sanctifier (in holiness Pentecostalism), Spirit-baptiser, healer and coming king
Divine healing and other spiritual gifts (prophecy, deliverance, miracles) as signs accompanying the preaching of the gospel
Urgent premillennial expectation of Christ’s return, making world evangelisation the task of the ‘latter rain’
Early belief that tongues were missionary languages (xenolalia), later reinterpreted as prayer and worship
Priesthood of all believers expressed in lay, women’s and young people’s ministry, though institutional churches later restricted women’s leadership
strategies: Independent ‘one-way ticket’ missionaries with little training or support, trusting divine provision
Spread through periodicals (The Apostolic Faith, Confidence, The Pentecostal Evangel) and networks of holiness missions
Healing campaigns and mass crusades emphasising signs and wonders
Indigenous-church principles: rapid training of national pastors and self-supporting churches (Hodges, AG Bible schools)
Lay evangelism by converts, open-air preaching and church planting in urban peripheries
Use of radio, television and later social media by national ministries

Authoritarian leadership cultures and alliances with authoritarian politicians in parts of Africa and Latin America

Opened leadership to lay people, the uneducated and (especially early) women
Created vigorous indigenous churches largely independent of Western control
Influenced all major traditions through the charismatic renewal, including Catholicism
Developed social ministries in education, rehabilitation and community development (documented by Miller and Yamamori)
Turned the global South into a major sender of missionaries
missions.outcome: Pentecostalism became the second-largest Christian grouping after Catholicism by many estimates, centred in the global South. Its missionary dynamism shifted from Western mission boards to national churches and transnational networks, carrying both renewal and controversy.

missions.name: Edinburgh 1910, the International Missionary Council and the World Council of Churches
missions.statusNote: The International Missionary Council was integrated into the World Council of Churches in 1961 as the Commission on World Mission and Evangelism, which still holds world mission conferences (Arusha 2018). The ecumenical missionary movement was transformed from a Western Protestant missionary alliance into a fellowship of churches, most of whose members are now in the global South, with much less emphasis on sending missionaries.
missions.summary: The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in June 1910, chaired by John R. Mott and organised by J. H. Oldham, sought to coordinate Protestant missions for ‘the evangelization of the world in this generation’. Its Continuation Committee became the International Missionary Council (1921), whose conferences at Jerusalem (1928), Tambaram (1938), Whitby (1947) and Willingen (1952) reshaped thinking on the indigenous church and the missio Dei. Merged into the World Council of Churches in 1961, the ecumenical stream broadened mission to include justice, dialogue and humanisation — a turn that provoked the evangelical–ecumenical split.
missions.story:
The World Missionary Conference met in the Assembly Hall of the United Free Church of Scotland in Edinburgh from 14 to 23 June 1910. Its 1,215 official delegates represented Protestant missionary societies — Anglican, Reformed, Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist and others — overwhelmingly from Britain, North America and continental Europe; fewer than twenty came from Asia and almost none from Africa. Roman Catholic and Orthodox missions were not represented, and to secure Anglo-Catholic participation the organisers excluded Latin America and other ‘Christian’ lands from the survey of fields. The eight commission reports surveyed the non-Christian world, the church on the mission field, education, other religions, missionary preparation, home base, government relations and cooperation. The most remembered speech was V. S. Azariah’s plea for genuine partnership: ‘You have given your goods to feed the poor. You have given your bodies to be burned. We also ask for love. Give us friends!’

Edinburgh’s Continuation Committee, with Mott as chair and Oldham as secretary, launched the International Review of Missions (1912), sponsored Mott’s 1912–13 tour of national conferences across Asia that led to national Christian councils, and survived the First World War, which shattered the confidence and internationalism of 1910 and saw German missions expelled from British territories. The International Missionary Council was formed at Lake Mohonk, New York, in 1921. At Jerusalem in 1928 it confronted secularism and the relationship between Christianity and other religions; the American Laymen’s Foreign Missions Inquiry (Re-Thinking Missions, 1932, chaired by W. E. Hocking) proposed that missions should seek common ground with other faiths and emphasise social service, provoking conservative outrage. At Tambaram, near Madras, in 1938 — the first conference at which delegates from the ‘younger churches’ were a majority — Hendrik Kraemer’s The Christian Message in a Non-Christian World argued for a ‘biblical realism’ discontinuous with other religions, against Indian theologians such as P. Chenchiah who sought continuity.

After 1945 the IMC reckoned with decolonisation. Whitby (1947) spoke of ‘partnership in obedience’ between older and younger churches. The expulsion of missionaries from China after 1949 forced a deep rethink, and at Willingen (1952) the idea of the missio Dei — that mission is first God’s own activity, in which the church participates — became central. Church unions such as the Church of South India (1947) embodied the conviction that division was a scandal on the mission field. The World Council of Churches, founded in Amsterdam in 1948 from the Faith and Order and Life and Work movements, absorbed the IMC at its New Delhi assembly in 1961, where Lesslie Newbigin argued for the integration of church and mission and the Russian and other Orthodox churches joined. Some evangelical missions and national councils, wary of the WCC, distanced themselves from the integration.

The 1960s shifted the agenda. The Mexico City conference (1963) spoke of ‘mission in six continents’, ending the idea that the West was only a sender. At Uppsala (1968) the WCC’s theme, ‘Behold, I make all things new’, and its study on ‘The Missionary Structure of the Congregation’ emphasised humanisation, development and the world as the arena of God’s action; Donald McGavran asked publicly ‘Will Uppsala betray the two billion?’ The Programme to Combat Racism (1969), with grants to southern African liberation movements, divided member churches. The Bangkok conference of the Commission on World Mission and Evangelism (December 1972–January 1973), on ‘Salvation Today’, defined salvation in personal, social, economic and political dimensions and gave voice to Third World churches’ anger at Western control; Kenyan Presbyterian leader John Gatu’s call (1971) for a temporary moratorium on foreign missionaries and funds was debated there and endorsed by the All Africa Conference of Churches at Lusaka in 1974.

Evangelicals saw these developments as a betrayal of Edinburgh’s evangelistic purpose and organised separately: the Wheaton Congress on the Church’s Worldwide Mission (April 1966), the Berlin World Congress on Evangelism (October–November 1966) and the Lausanne Congress (1974). The ecumenical side, for its part, criticised evangelicals for neglecting justice and for complicity with Western power. Later ecumenical documents sought a balance: Mission and Evangelism: An Ecumenical Affirmation (1982), the conferences at Melbourne (1980, ‘Your Kingdom Come’, on the poor) and San Antonio (1989), and Together Towards Life (2012), which spoke of ‘mission from the margins’. In 2010 the centenary of Edinburgh was marked by a conference that, unlike 1910, included Catholics, Orthodox, Pentecostals and evangelicals.

Historians such as Brian Stanley regard Edinburgh 1910 as both the high-water mark of Western missionary confidence — sure that Christianity and Western civilisation would together transform the world — and the starting point of modern ecumenism. Its successors made real gains in indigenous leadership, church union and theology of mission, but the movement also lost much of its missionary-sending energy, and mainline missionary numbers fell sharply from the 1960s while evangelical and Pentecostal sending grew.

missions.name: Bible translation movement (British & Foreign Bible Society, Wycliffe/SIL)
missions.statusNote: Bible societies (coordinated by the United Bible Societies since 1946) and the Wycliffe Global Alliance and SIL Global continue to translate; by the mid-2020s Wycliffe reported a full Bible in more than 700 languages and at least some Scripture in over 3,700, with translation increasingly led by national translators and local churches. missions.summary: From the founding of the British and Foreign Bible Society in 1804 to Wycliffe Bible Translators and the Summer Institute of Linguistics in the twentieth century, Protestant missions made vernacular Bible translation a central task. Bible societies printed and distributed Scriptures through colporteurs across Europe, Asia and Africa; Cameron Townsend’s Wycliffe/SIL trained linguists to reduce unwritten languages to writing and translate the New Testament. Scholars such as Lamin Sanneh credit translation with revitalising local languages and cultures, while critics accuse SIL of serving states, oil companies and assimilation.
missions.story:
The British and Foreign Bible Society was founded in London on 7 March 1804 by evangelical Anglicans and Dissenters, including members of the Clapham Sect; the much-told story of the Welsh girl Mary Jones walking to Bala for a Bible from Thomas Charles became its founding legend. Its purpose was to circulate Scripture ‘without note or comment’, a rule that allowed Anglicans and Nonconformists to cooperate. Sister societies followed — the American Bible Society (1816), the Netherlands and Russian Bible Societies (1813–14) and many auxiliaries in India, beginning at Calcutta in 1811. The BFBS funded missionary translators such as William Carey’s team at Serampore, Henry Martyn (Urdu and Persian New Testaments), Robert Morrison (Chinese Bible, 1823) and Samuel Crowther (Yoruba), and employed colporteurs such as George Borrow in Spain (1835–40) to sell Bibles in Catholic and Orthodox lands, provoking official hostility.

The nineteenth-century societies made the Bible the most translated book in the world. Disputes accompanied the growth: the Apocrypha controversy of 1825–26 led Scottish auxiliaries to secede when the BFBS refused to fund Bibles including the deuterocanonical books, and debates over terms for God in Chinese (Shangdi versus Shen) divided missionaries for decades. Translation required missionaries to create alphabets, grammars and dictionaries, often with indigenous collaborators whose contributions were seldom acknowledged. By 1900 the BFBS had issued Scripture in over 400 languages and its sales ran to millions of copies a year.

The twentieth-century translation movement was shaped by William Cameron Townsend, who went to Guatemala in 1917 to sell Spanish Bibles and was challenged by a Kaqchikel man, reportedly asking why, if God was so great, he did not speak Kaqchikel. Townsend completed a Kaqchikel New Testament in 1931 and in 1934 founded ‘Camp Wycliffe’ in Arkansas to train translators. From it grew the Summer Institute of Linguistics (SIL) and Wycliffe Bible Translators (incorporated 1942). Townsend secured contracts with the Mexican government under Lázaro Cárdenas (1936) and later with Peru (1946), Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, the Philippines and Papua New Guinea, presenting SIL as a scientific and educational body serving national literacy programmes. Kenneth Pike and Eugene Nida, both linked to SIL, became leading linguists; Nida, working for the American Bible Society, developed the theory of ‘dynamic equivalence’ (Toward a Science of Translating, 1964), which shaped popular translations worldwide. The aviation and radio service JAARS (1948) supported translators in remote areas.

SIL’s methods produced controversy. Its work with the Huaorani in Ecuador — after five missionaries (not SIL members) were killed in 1956 in ‘Operation Auca’, Rachel Saint, Townsend’s colleague, lived among them — involved resettling many Huaorani into a protectorate in the 1960s–70s, which critics such as David Stoll linked to the opening of the region to oil companies. In the 1970s–80s anthropologists and nationalist governments accused SIL of cultural destruction, collaboration with US interests and evangelism disguised as linguistics. Mexico ended its agreement in 1979, Ecuador ordered SIL’s departure in 1981, Panama and Brazil restricted its work, and in Colombia guerrillas murdered the SIL member Chester Bitterman in 1981. Supporters respond that SIL documented hundreds of endangered languages, published the Ethnologue (from 1951) and promoted mother-tongue literacy.

After 1945 the Bible societies formed the United Bible Societies (1946) and, following the Second Vatican Council’s call for vernacular Scripture (Dei Verbum, 1965), agreed Guidelines for Interconfessional Cooperation in Translating the Bible with the Catholic Church (1968), producing common translations in many languages. In 1999 Wycliffe adopted ‘Vision 2025’, aiming to begin a translation in every language that needed one by 2025. Computer tools (Paratext), oral and sign-language translation, and national organisations — the Wycliffe Global Alliance includes agencies such as the Nigeria Bible Translation Trust and the Indian Institute for Cross-Cultural Communication — have shifted leadership to the global South. A dispute in 2011–12 over translating ‘Son of God’ in Muslim contexts led to an external review by the World Evangelical Alliance (2012–13) and strained relations with some supporting denominations.

Historians increasingly see translation as one of missions’ most consequential legacies. Lamin Sanneh and Andrew Walls argued that by translating the Bible into local languages missionaries implicitly affirmed those languages and cultures, stimulating literary standardisation, national identity and later resistance to colonial rule — in contrast to Islam’s use of untranslated Arabic scripture. Critics note that standardisation could privilege one dialect, that translation was entangled with colonial power and that some translations imported foreign concepts. Both sides agree that most of the world’s written literature in many minority languages began with Bible translation.

missions.summary: After 1945 conservative evangelicals, increasingly estranged from the ecumenical movement, built their own global mission networks around Billy Graham, Christianity Today and new agencies. The Wheaton and Berlin congresses of 1966 led to the International Congress on World Evangelization at Lausanne in July 1974, whose Covenant, drafted by John Stott, reaffirmed the priority of evangelism while confessing evangelical neglect of social responsibility. Ralph Winter’s call to reach ‘hidden’ or unreached peoples and later the ‘10/40 window’ reshaped evangelical strategy.
missions.story:
Post-war American evangelicalism, organised in the National Association of Evangelicals (1942) and its Evangelical Foreign Missions Association (1945), alongside the older Interdenominational Foreign Mission Association (1917), sent a flood of missionaries into the world after the Second World War — many of them veterans who had seen Asia and Africa during the war. Billy Graham’s crusades, from Los Angeles (1949) and Harringay in London (1954) to New York (1957), Australia (1959) and Seoul (1973, where over a million attended the final service on Yoido Plaza), made him the movement’s public face. Christianity Today (1956), Fuller Theological Seminary (1947) and agencies such as World Vision (1950) and Campus Crusade for Christ (1951) built an evangelical infrastructure that consciously stood apart from the World Council of Churches.

Two congresses in 1966 marked the separation. The Congress on the Church’s Worldwide Mission at Wheaton College (April 1966), sponsored by the IFMA and EFMA, issued the Wheaton Declaration, which criticised the WCC’s theological pluralism and universalism while confessing evangelical failures in social concern and cooperation. The World Congress on Evangelism in Berlin (October–November 1966), convened by Christianity Today with Carl F. H. Henry as chair and Graham as honorary chair, gathered some 1,200 delegates from about 100 countries under the theme ‘One Race, One Gospel, One Task’. Regional congresses followed in Singapore (1968), Minneapolis (1969), Bogotá (1969) and Amsterdam (1971), widening participation from the global South.

The International Congress on World Evangelization met at the Palais de Beaulieu, Lausanne, from 16 to 25 July 1974, with about 2,700 participants from some 150 countries, nearly half from the global South. Ralph Winter’s address argued that most non-Christians — some 2.7 billion people — lived in ‘hidden peoples’ with no church able to evangelise them by near-neighbour witness, so that cross-cultural mission remained essential. The Latin Americans René Padilla and Samuel Escobar delivered plenary papers criticising an evangelicalism tied to American culture, consumerism and the ‘American way of life’, and calling for a gospel that addressed poverty and injustice; about 500 participants signed a ‘Theology and Implications of Radical Discipleship’ statement. The Lausanne Covenant, drafted by a committee chaired by John Stott, stated (paragraph 5) that ‘evangelism and socio-political involvement are both part of our Christian duty’ and expressed penitence for having sometimes regarded them as mutually exclusive, while affirming (paragraph 6) that ‘in the church’s mission of sacrificial service evangelism is primary’. Paragraph 9 addressed the moratorium debate from Bangkok, accepting that ‘a reduction of foreign missionaries and money in an evangelized country may sometimes be necessary’ to promote the national church’s growth in self-reliance.

The balance between evangelism and social action continued to divide the movement. Graham, Winter and Donald McGavran wanted the Lausanne Committee for World Evangelization (formed 1974) to focus on evangelism; Stott, Padilla, Escobar and others insisted on the Covenant’s wider vision. The 1977 Pasadena consultation on the homogeneous unit principle, the Willowbank consultation on gospel and culture (1978), the Consultation on World Evangelization at Pattaya (1980) — where a group of participants protested the neglect of social issues — and the Grand Rapids consultation on Evangelism and Social Responsibility (1982), which described social action as a consequence of, bridge to and partner of evangelism, each worked through the tension. Latin American evangelicals of the Fraternidad Teológica Latinoamericana (1970) developed ‘misión integral’, later carried into the Micah Network (1999). Lausanne II in Manila (1989) produced the Manila Manifesto and launched the AD2000 and Beyond Movement, in which Luis Bush popularised the ‘10/40 window’ (1990) — the band from 10° to 40° north of the equator from West Africa to East Asia containing most unevangelised peoples.

The unreached-peoples paradigm, institutionalised in Winter’s U.S. Center for World Mission (Pasadena, 1976), the Perspectives course and the Joshua Project database, redirected evangelical sending toward Muslim, Hindu and Buddhist peoples and encouraged ‘insider movements’ and church-planting movements. Its critics argued that it reduced mission to managerial targets, used military metaphors, encouraged spiritual-warfare ‘mapping’ of territorial spirits (questioned by a Lausanne statement in 1993) and provoked hostility in countries sensitive to proselytism. Lausanne III at Cape Town (2010), with over 4,000 participants from 198 countries, issued the Cape Town Commitment, drafted largely by Christopher Wright, which framed mission in terms of love for God, neighbour and creation. Lausanne 4 in Seoul-Incheon (2024) issued the Seoul Statement, whose sections on human sexuality and other matters were criticised by some as narrowing the movement’s agenda.

Historians such as Brian Stanley see Lausanne as the moment when evangelicalism became a global, rather than Anglo-American, movement, with majority-world voices reshaping its theology. Its achievements include a broadly accepted evangelical statement of mission and a lasting network; its weaknesses include dependence on Western money, recurrent tensions between strategists and theologians, and an emphasis on quantifiable ‘closure’ that some see as eroding the Covenant’s holistic vision.

missions.name: Church Growth and people movements (Pickett, McGavran)
missions.statusNote: As a named school the Church Growth movement peaked between the 1960s and 1980s. It was transformed into church-planting movement strategies, megachurch and ‘seeker-sensitive’ methods in the West, and (through C. Peter Wagner) the signs-and-wonders and New Apostolic Reformation networks; its homogeneous-unit principle is now widely criticised.
missions.summary: The Church Growth movement grew from J. Waskom Pickett’s study of Dalit mass movements in India (1933) and Donald McGavran’s argument in The Bridges of God (1955) that peoples become Christian most readily through group decisions within their own social units. Institutionalised at Fuller Theological Seminary’s School of World Mission (1965), it used social science to measure and promote church growth and taught the controversial homogeneous-unit principle.
missions.story:
The movement’s roots lie in India. Between the 1870s and 1930s hundreds of thousands of Dalits — Chuhras in Punjab, Malas and Madigas in Andhra — became Christian in ‘mass movements’ that many missionaries distrusted as motivated by material gain. The Methodist missionary J. Waskom Pickett, commissioned by the National Christian Council, surveyed these movements and published Christian Mass Movements in India (1933), arguing that group conversions were often deeper and more stable than individual ones because converts were not cut off from their kin. Pickett’s data influenced Bishop Azariah of Dornakal and Donald McGavran, a Disciples of Christ missionary born in India to missionary parents, who arrived as a missionary in 1923, later worked among the Satnamis of Chhattisgarh, and was frustrated by the slow growth of mission-station churches. With Pickett and others he co-authored Church Growth and Group Conversion (1936).

McGavran’s The Bridges of God (1955) contrasted the ‘mission station approach’, which extracted individuals from their communities, with ‘people movements’ in which families, clans or castes turned to Christ together. He urged missions to concentrate resources on ‘receptive’ peoples. In 1961 he founded the Institute of Church Growth at Northwest Christian College in Eugene, Oregon, and in 1965 became founding dean of the School of World Mission at Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena, joined by Alan Tippett, Ralph Winter, Charles Kraft, Arthur Glasser and C. Peter Wagner. Understanding Church Growth (1970) became the movement’s textbook, distinguishing ‘discipling’ (bringing a people to Christian allegiance) from ‘perfecting’ (later growth in holiness).

The most contested idea was the homogeneous-unit principle: in McGavran’s words, ‘people like to become Christians without crossing racial, linguistic, or class barriers’. Church Growth advocates presented this as a description of how conversion happens and as a strategy for evangelism, not as an ideal for the church. Critics in India, Latin America and the United States argued that it baptised caste and racial segregation. In 1977 the Lausanne Theology and Education Group held a consultation at Pasadena on the principle, recording sharp disagreement; René Padilla’s essay ‘The Unity of the Church and the Homogeneous Unit Principle’ (1982) argued that the New Testament church deliberately united Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free. Wagner’s Our Kind of People (1979) defended homogeneous churches in the United States, a position he later partly modified.

Church Growth also became a major force in North American church life. Win Arn’s Institute for American Church Growth (1972), Wagner’s writings and the American Society for Church Growth (1985) applied its methods — demographic research, attention to ‘receptivity’, goal-setting — to suburban congregations, contributing to the megachurch and seeker-sensitive movements of the 1980s–90s. In 1982 Wagner and John Wimber taught a Fuller course (MC510) on ‘signs, wonders and church growth’ that sparked controversy at the seminary and led Wagner into the ‘Third Wave’ and later the New Apostolic Reformation, a direction far removed from McGavran’s.

Critics within and outside evangelicalism faulted the movement for numerical pragmatism, for measuring success by membership statistics, for separating evangelism from justice (the ‘discipling’ and ‘perfecting’ split), and for treating social sciences uncritically. In India its emphasis on caste-based people movements was blamed by some for entrenching caste divisions within churches. McGavran in turn criticised the ecumenical movement, asking in 1968 whether Uppsala would ‘betray the two billion’ unevangelised, and his insistence that the unfinished evangelistic task must remain central helped shape the Lausanne Congress.

The movement’s lasting legacy lies in its people-group thinking, which fed Winter’s unreached-peoples paradigm and later church-planting movement (CPM) and Disciple-Making Movement strategies, and in its insistence that mission be evaluated by whether churches actually grow. Its sociological realism about group conversion is broadly accepted by historians of Indian and African Christianity, while its homogeneous-unit principle remains one of the most criticised ideas in modern missiology.

missions.name: Youth and mobilisation movements (OM, YWAM, Urbana, short-term missions)
missions.statusNote: OM and YWAM operate in well over 100 countries each, with large majority-world staff; Urbana continues triennially (now in St Louis). Short-term mission trips remain a mass phenomenon among Western and increasingly Korean, Brazilian and African churches, though research and criticism since the 2000s have pushed many agencies to reform practices.
missions.summary: From the 1940s evangelical student conventions and new youth agencies turned mission into an experience for hundreds of thousands of young people. InterVarsity’s Urbana conventions (from 1946), George Verwer’s Operation Mobilisation (1957) with its ships Logos and Doulos, and Loren Cunningham’s Youth With A Mission (1960) pioneered short-term service, which by the 2000s involved well over a million American church members a year. The movement greatly widened participation but has been criticised for ‘voluntourism’, dependency and harm to host communities.
missions.story:
After the Second World War student evangelicals revived the Student Volunteer Movement’s tradition of mission conventions. InterVarsity Christian Fellowship held its first student missionary convention in Toronto in December 1946, and from 1948 at the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign; ‘Urbana’ became a triennial gathering often attended by 15,000–20,000 students, with John Stott, Billy Graham and majority-world speakers. Campus Crusade for Christ (Bill Bright, 1951), the Navigators and the International Fellowship of Evangelical Students (1947) multiplied campus ministries that fed recruits to missions.

Operation Mobilisation began when George Verwer, converted at a Billy Graham rally in 1955, took fellow students to Mexico in 1957 to distribute Gospel literature. OM organised summer campaigns in Europe from 1961 and sent teams overland by truck to India from 1963–64, where it became one of the largest agencies; OM India (now partly independent) worked especially in the north and among Dalits. Verwer’s emphasis on radical discipleship and ‘revolution of love’ appealed to young volunteers. OM bought the ship Logos in 1970 and Doulos in 1977, floating book fairs that visited ports across Asia, Africa and Latin America; Logos was wrecked in the Beagle Channel in 1988 without loss of life, and Logos Hope entered service in 2009.

Youth With A Mission grew from a vision Loren Cunningham, an Assemblies of God youth leader, reported having in the Bahamas in 1956 of waves of young people covering the continents. Founded in 1960, YWAM sent short-term teams to the Caribbean and in 1969 opened a School of Evangelism in Lausanne, Switzerland; its campus at Kona, Hawaii, became the University of the Nations (1978), and Mercy Ships (from 1978) provided hospital ships. Charismatic in ethos, YWAM grew to thousands of staff and the Discipleship Training School model, combining teaching with outreach. It eventually separated from Assemblies of God sponsorship and became a decentralised network.

The short-term model spread far beyond these agencies. From the 1980s congregations, schools and denominations sent youth groups and adults on one- or two-week trips to build houses, run vacation Bible schools or hold medical clinics, especially in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and later Africa. Surveys reported by Robert Priest and Robert Wuthnow in the 2000s estimated that around 1.5–2 million Americans took part each year, at an annual cost often estimated in the billions of dollars. Korean, Brazilian, Nigerian and Indian churches adopted the model, and mobilisation courses such as Perspectives on the World Christian Movement linked short-term experience with long-term unreached-peoples strategy.

The model drew increasing criticism. Research found little measurable long-term change in participants’ giving or mission commitment; hosts reported that teams consumed local hospitality, displaced paid local labour, created dependency and reinforced ideas of Western superiority. Orphanage tourism in Haiti, Cambodia, Uganda and Nepal encouraged the institutionalisation of children who had living parents. Books such as When Helping Hurts (Corbett and Fikkert, 2009) and Standards of Excellence in Short-Term Mission (2003) urged partnership with local churches, preparation and long-term relationships. Within the youth agencies, some former members have alleged spiritual abuse, authoritarian leadership and safeguarding failures at particular bases.

By the 2020s mobilisation movements were among the most globalised parts of evangelical mission: the majority of OM and YWAM workers came from outside North America and Europe, and short-term teams increasingly travelled ‘from everywhere to everywhere’. Supporters credit them with recruiting a large share of long-term missionaries and with exposing churches to world Christianity; critics see them as a consumerist distortion of mission that can do real harm when poorly designed.
